articles.title: ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone
articles.summary: It would be nice to say that Connor Storrie burns up the screen in “April X,” the star’s first film vehicle released since TV’s “Heated Rivalry” made him hot property, but it would be overstating the case.
body: Shot before 'Heated Rivalry' launched its leading man to stardom, Michel K. Parandi's murky futuristic thriller will only be remembered — if at all — for that fortunate casting coup.

The year is unspecified, but the fatigued brutalist housing blocks of outer Bucharest are still standing: Though it doesn’t specify a location either, “April X” uses the present-day wear and tear of the Romanian capital, where the film was shot on location, as shorthand for a world collapsing into concrete ruin. The odd hi-tech drone adds some futuristic pizzazz to the film’s exterior vistas, but the new technologies defining the narrative aren’t of the gleaming, brave-new-world variety: People are being cloned in grubby, shadowed fashion, while memories and dreams can be captured and downloaded onto surprisingly retro-looking data devices.

articles.title: Behemoth! review - Pedro Pascal classical music drama hits all the wrong notes
articles.summary: New York film festival: The actor stumbles through Tony Gilroy’s forgettable film marred by stylistic gimmicks. Tony Gilroy has built a sturdy career as the director of the Bourne films and show runner of the popular Star Wars spin-off Andor.
body: As the first feature film he has directed since 2012’s The Bourne Legacy, the classical music drama Behemoth! promised to be an intriguing return from a master of threading the needle between slick action and deeply felt drama. His new film comes with a score from nine A-list composers who have banded together and called themselves The Behemoth! Collective, a stacked cast and a womanizing central character who looks phenomenal in a tux: “ Tár for straight men”, as a friend of mine put it.

If only Pedro Pascal had an iota of Cate Blanchett’s charisma or Gilroy came close to Todd Field’s elegant braiding of genres. Our protagonist is Alex (Pascal), an inscrutable cello maestro who has moved home to Los Angeles after nearly two decades on the road. The city offers him regular, if soulless, session work scoring TV shows and movies, as well as the opportunity to be closer to his brother (Will Arnett) and mother, a respected harpist who is suffering from ill health.

articles.title: Film festival aims to celebrate British-Latino identity
articles.summary: The Latino film festival in the capital will screen 60 films from 27 countries over five days.
body: A film festival billed as London's only competitive Latino film festival is now under way, with 60 films from 27 countries showing over five days at venues including the Barbican, the ICA, Ciné Lumière and BFI Stephen Street.
Guests include Cuban dancer Carlos Acosta, a former principal at the Royal Ballet, Argentine actor Óscar Martínez, Cuban actor Jorge Perugorría and Oscar-winning Chilean screenwriter Gonzalo Maza.
The event was founded by Cuban actress Ketty Rodriguez who, when she moved to London, was struck by the lack of Latin representation in a city famous for its multiculturalism, film and history.
Rodriguez says it is the first competitive Latino film festival of this size in London.

articles.title: New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: A festival launching Oct. 11 at Manhattan’s SVA Theatre is positioning itself as an answer to the flattened, stereotyped picture of Muslims Western media often traffics in.
body: “This festival exists because those stories deserve a stage in this city, not on the margins of someone else’s,” said Nawal Mubin, the festival’s co-founder and director.
The day will open with a reception for filmmakers and industry guests. Two blocks of six films each, running roughly an hour apiece, will precede the awards and the jury announcement.

Emmy winner Aasif Mandvi, a longtime “The Daily Show” correspondent who also starred in Paramount+ series “Evil,” sits on the six-member jury. He is joined by Arab-American writer-director Darine Hotait, founder of Cinephilia Productions, whose shorts have aired on HBO, AMC, SundanceTV and the BBC; Munir Atalla, head of production and acquisitions at Watermelon Pictures and a former Netflix creative executive; and producer Abubakar Khan, whose resume includes “The Glassworker,” Pakistan’s entry for the 2024 Oscars, and SXSW 2023 audience award winner “Mustache.”

articles.title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic
articles.summary: New York Film Festival: The Geese frontman mesmerizes in a concert film that is both swoony and austere. One night last December, weary from a busy week and the impending doom of winter, I hurried into Carnegie Hall to witness Cameron Winter.
body: So far, in fact, that I assumed the maybe-camera that came on stage at one point was a bit, perhaps a jab at our incessant need to film things from a very deadpan celebrity whose only non-music interlude that evening was to wordlessly stand, stretch and mockingly fight with the stage door, as if trying to escape his own momentous show. I emerged from the event teary, charged by what felt like a communion across time, and confused by a friend’s text: “can’t wait for the cameron winter PTA doc”.

The on-stage camera notwithstanding, Anderson et al largely stay out of the way, appearing to lurk throughout the cavernous theater, from my rafter seat to the aisle to the piano bench, like one of Winter’s many shadows, themselves filmed to haunting effect. Depending on the scene, the stark shifts in light, and the angle of piercingly close shots on his face, Winter appears either 20 or 60 – all the better to get hit by his absurd yet evocative lyrics, such nonsense as “the beach ball cathedral dimpled like a sea fly swarming”, “until the conga line behind me is a thousand chickens long” and, most evocatively for a largely secular New York audience, “god is real.”

articles.title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Is a Classical Cellist Skating Through a Midlife Crisis in Tony Gilroy’s Elevated Bauble of a Music Drama
articles.summary: "Behemoth!" is a classical-musician movie. It’s a midlife-crisis movie. It’s a romantic mystery. It’s Tony Gilroy fiddling around with pure movie form.
body: It understands the classical-music world and has fun fiddling around with film form. But is that enough?

The conductors who oversee the recording of the movie scores are portrayed as hyper-demanding corporate perfectionists. (One of them, a prima donna played by Thomas Kretschmann, makes it feel like you’re seeing Klaus Kinski going to work for Skydance.) And from the film’s opening scene, which immerses us in the lingo of rehearsal, which is a mixture of old-school classical Euro directives (“pianissimo”) and Hollywood jargon (“new ink”), we’re right there in the cavernous recording studio, feeling the heat and the nuance.

Alex, after the debacle of his break-up with Wilde’s clingy diva in Chicago, returns to Los Angeles, where he grew up. He can get session work there, and does. He still seems mellow, but he’s bestirred by a pet obsession: listening to the original avant-pop compositions posted online by Viviana ( Alexa Swinton ), a 15-year-old girl who has become a local celebrity. It turns out that he’s got a connection to her; she’s Nadia’s daughter. But why is he so interested? He’s just got…a feeling.

articles.title: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversary
articles.summary: Ahead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made now.
body: I t is one of the prime minister’s all-time favourite films and has endured in the hearts of the British public since it was released in 1996. Ostensibly a story about a small town colliery band’s journey to the finals of Britain’s biggest brass band competition at the Royal Albert Hall, Brassed Off is unashamedly political.

“I think the people who went expecting a political film got the bonus of a bit of a comedy,” says its writer, Mark Herman, three decades on. “And the people who went expecting comedy got the bonus of the political message. I think anybody who went got a sort of bonus they might not have expected.

“On the face of it, a brass band film is not an easy pitch but word of mouth really rolled and suddenly it went on and on in places for months,” he recalls. “I thought it might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley for about two weeks,” laughs Herman. “So yeah, it’s amazing.”

articles.title: Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises?
articles.summary: Big moments from headline acts are shared online long before many fans see their favourite artists.
body: Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.
You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view.
When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings.
But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.

articles.title: All 5 Anne Hathaway Movie Performances From 2026, Ranked
articles.summary: Anne Hathaway has had an incredible year, appearing in five distinctly different movies. Here's a ranking of all of her 2026 performances, from worst to best.
body: In 2014, we hit the zenith of the so-called "McConnaissance," a re-evaluation and return to form for Matthew McConaughey that won him an Oscar and rave reviews for his work on the first season of "True Detective." In 2024, Josh Hartnett got a well-deserved critical reappraisal thanks to his work the previous year in "Oppenheimer" and then his deliciously deranged M. Night Shyamalan thriller "Trap." Now, we're in the thick of 2026, and it is, without contest, the year of Anne Hathaway.

Let me be abundantly clear: Even in bad movies, Hathaway is reliably good. In fact, I'd go so far as to say that Hathaway has confirmed, this year, that she's one of our finest performers by a mile. Still, some of her performances this year are better than the others, and that's where I come in. Here are all of Hathaway's 2026 film performances, ranked.

articles.title: Traitors claim their first victim as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin
articles.summary: There was a murder and a recruitment in the latest episode, and that was just in the opening minutes.
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the second episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
A comedian, a journalist, an actor and a TV presenter walk into a church. But sadly, the punchline for one of them was becoming the first victim of this year's Celebrity Traitors.
As Friday's episode got under way, a delicious new twist saw traitors Richard E Grant and Maya Jama invite James Acaster to join them in the turret, and simultaneously murder a fellow player.
Unfortunately, it fell to Amol Rajan to become the Paloma Faith of this series - being taken away in a coffin in episode two before even having the chance to take part in a banishment.
